items.title: How tape changed composition
items.claim: Magnetic tape recording became widely available in the late 1940s. Which composer used it to develop musique concrete in 1948?
items.reveal_title: Schaeffer's Etude aux chemins de fer, 1948
items.reveal:
Schaeffer used recorded train sounds to compose at RTF, Paris. The studio later became GRM (Groupe de Recherches Musicales).

The method established sound itself, separated from its source, as compositional material.
items.why: Recording media are not just preservation tools; they create new compositional possibilities.

items.title: When Vivaldi was rediscovered
items.claim: After Vivaldi's death in 1741 his music largely disappeared from concert programmes. When did serious revival begin?

options.text: Within ten years of his death
The 1920s-1950s, after manuscript discoveries in Turin

items.reveal:
Manuscripts found in monastic libraries reached the Biblioteca Nazionale di Torino in the 1920s-1930s. Recording, especially after 1950, restored Vivaldi to the canon.

The Four Seasons (1725) is now among the most recorded works in classical music.
items.why: Canonical status is reconstructed, not fixed; archival luck matters.

items.title: The Mozart effect
items.claim: The 'Mozart effect' became famous after a 1993 Nature paper. What did the original study actually report?

options.text: Listening to Mozart permanently raised children's IQ
A short, narrow improvement on a spatial reasoning task in adults, lasting about 10-15 minutes

items.reveal_title: A short-lived effect on one specific task in adults
items.reveal:
Rauscher, Shaw and Ky (1993) reported a brief improvement on the Stanford-Binet paper-folding task in adult students.

The finding became 'classical music makes babies smarter' in popular media; later meta-analyses (Pietschnig et al., 2010) found little support for that broader claim.
items.why: Translating a careful experimental finding into public policy often loses its caveats.
